name: Physics-Informed Learning
plain_language_definition: Physics-informed learning trains models while constraining them with known governing equations, conservation laws, boundary conditions, or residual penalties.
ordinary_problem: Pure black-box models can fit data while violating physics, especially when measurements are sparse or extrapolation matters.
naive_picture: The naive view is that a neural network can simply replace a simulator once enough data is available.
why_naive_fails: Physical simulation problems mix equations, data, discretization, stability, uncertainty, and scientific validity. A generic ML benchmark can hide failures that matter in the real system.
first_principles: If the physical law is known, learning should search among functions that are consistent with that law rather than treating every data point as unconstrained supervision.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, it is easy to build a model that looks accurate on examples but fails under new parameters, longer time horizons, or scientific constraints.
course_role: This theme organizes DDPS seminars related to physics-informed learning and gives us a first-pass route for later deep dives.

name: Reduced-Order Modeling
plain_language_definition: Reduced-order modeling builds lower-dimensional surrogates of expensive physical simulations while preserving the dominant dynamics needed for prediction or control.
ordinary_problem: High-fidelity simulations can be too slow for design loops, optimization, uncertainty quantification, or real-time control.
naive_picture: The naive view is that a neural network can simply replace a simulator once enough data is available.
why_naive_fails: Physical simulation problems mix equations, data, discretization, stability, uncertainty, and scientific validity. A generic ML benchmark can hide failures that matter in the real system.
first_principles: If the system's important states live near a lower-dimensional structure, computation can focus on that structure instead of repeatedly solving the full problem.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, it is easy to build a model that looks accurate on examples but fails under new parameters, longer time horizons, or scientific constraints.
course_role: This theme organizes DDPS seminars related to reduced-order modeling and gives us a first-pass route for later deep dives.

name: Differentiable Simulation
plain_language_definition: Differentiable simulation exposes gradients through a simulator so parameters, controls, shapes, or models can be optimized using gradient-based methods.

first_principles: If a simulator maps causes to effects, differentiating that map tells us how to change the causes to improve the effect.

name: Operator Learning
plain_language_definition: Operator learning trains models to map between functions, such as from initial conditions or coefficients to full solution fields.
ordinary_problem: A simulator often needs to solve a family of related PDE problems, not just predict one fixed vector output.

first_principles: When inputs and outputs are functions, the learned object should approximate the solution operator that transforms one function into another.

name: Fluid Mechanics Simulation
plain_language_definition: Fluid mechanics simulation models flows, shocks, turbulence, and conservation laws using numerical methods, learned surrogates, or hybrid methods.
ordinary_problem: Fluids create multiscale, nonlinear, instability-prone dynamics that are costly to simulate and difficult to learn robustly.
naive_picture: The naive view is that a neural network can simply replace a simulator once enough data is available.
why_naive_fails: Physical simulation problems mix equations, data, discretization, stability, uncertainty, and scientific validity. A generic ML benchmark can hide failures that matter in the real system.
first_principles: A flow model must respect transport, conservation, stability, and scale interactions; otherwise small errors can propagate into wrong dynamics.

name: Hybrid Twins
plain_language_definition: Hybrid twins combine mechanistic simulation with learned components and live data to represent, predict, and update physical systems.

name: Scientific Machine Learning
plain_language_definition: Scientific machine learning uses ML to accelerate, infer, control, or augment models of physical, biological, and engineering systems.
ordinary_problem: Scientific problems often have limited data, strong priors, expensive simulators, and high penalties for physically invalid predictions.

first_principles: The learning problem should be designed around the scientific structure: equations, symmetries, measurements, uncertainty, and the decision the model will support.

name: Uncertainty And Robustness
plain_language_definition: Uncertainty and robustness address whether learned simulation models remain reliable under sparse data, out-of-distribution parameters, numerical error, and long rollouts.
ordinary_problem: A surrogate can be accurate on average yet fail exactly where scientific or engineering decisions are most sensitive.
naive_picture: The naive view is that a neural network can simply replace a simulator once enough data is available.
why_naive_fails: Physical simulation problems mix equations, data, discretization, stability, uncertainty, and scientific validity. A generic ML benchmark can hide failures that matter in the real system.
first_principles: A model should communicate what it knows, remain stable under perturbations, and be tested where errors would change the conclusion.

name: Inverse Problems And Control
plain_language_definition: Inverse problems and control use observations or objectives to infer hidden parameters, states, forces, designs, or interventions.
ordinary_problem: In practice we often observe effects and need to recover causes, or choose actions that make a physical system behave a desired way.
